course.title: Observability & telemetry math
course.description: Observability reps for the operate-it part of a system-design interview: solving a trace-sampling rate inversely from a storage budget, the metric-cardinality product that turns one unbounded label into a budget incident, tiering log retention by age, error-budget burn rates and the hours until the budget is gone, the on-call toil that false pages burn, instrumentation overhead as a share of request latency, how scrape resolution drives the points a time-series database must hold, and which traces head versus tail sampling actually keep. Every drill is whole-number arithmetic with the conversions named (86,400 s/day; 720 h in a 30-day month; money in integer cents; per-mille = parts per thousand = x/1000), so you practise the reasoning, not the calculator.

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · cost  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "We serve 20,000 requests/s and our tracing contract covers 8,640,000 stored traces a day. What sampling rate do we configure, and how many traces per second does that keep?"

**Why it works.** A probabilistic sampler keeps a fixed per-mille of requests (‰ = x/1000), so kept traces per second are qps × sample‰ ÷ 1000. The day produces qps × 86,400 traces (86,400 s/day), so the dial a budget allows is the budget divided by that, scaled by 1000. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `tracesKeptPerSec(qps, samplePermille)` → `qps × samplePermille ÷ 1000`
- `samplePermilleForBudget(budgetTracesPerDay, qps)` → `budgetTracesPerDay × 1000 ÷ (qps × 86400)`

**Worked example.** 20,000 QPS at 5‰ → 20,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = **100** traces kept per second.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
The sampling dial is set by the budget, not by curiosity.

For `samplePermilleForBudget(8640000, 20000)`:
- the day produces 20,000 × 86,400 = 1,728,000,000 traces
- the budget stores 8,640,000 of them
- 8,640,000 × 1000 ÷ 1,728,000,000 = **5‰**

Module 09's `dlq-sizing` sizes a per-mille slice of FAILURES you do not choose; here the slice is a CHOICE you solve for inversely from what you can afford to store.
hints: Work backwards: how many traces does the day produce in total, and what fraction of them fits the allowance?
kept/s = qps × p ÷ 1000; p = budget × 1000 ÷ (qps × 86,400).
Kept traces are qps × sample‰ ÷ 1000 — to size the dial from a budget, divide the day's stored-trace allowance by the day's total requests (qps × 86,400) and scale by 1000

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · cost  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our request-count metric has three labels: status (5 values), endpoint (20) and pod (10). A teammate wants to add a user-id label with 50,000 values. How many time series does that create, and what does it cost at 2¢ per series per month?"

**Why it works.** A time-series database stores one series per distinct combination of label values, so in the worst case the series count is the PRODUCT of every label's distinct-value count. A metric with no labels is exactly one series (the empty product is 1). Billing is per active series, so the bill is the series count × cents per series (money in integer cents).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `seriesCount(labelCardinalities)` → the product of the array (`1` for an empty array)
- `monthlySeriesCents(labelCardinalities, centsPerSeries)` → `seriesCount(…) × centsPerSeries`

**Worked example.** Labels of 5, 20 and 10 values → 5 × 20 × 10 = **1,000** series.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
Cardinality is multiplicative, so one unbounded label dominates everything.

For `seriesCount([5, 20, 10, 50000])`:
- 5 statuses × 20 endpoints × 10 pods = 1,000 series
- × a user-id label with 50,000 values → **50,000,000** series
- at 2¢ each that is 100,000,000¢ ($1M) a month

One unbounded label is a budget incident — module 08's `loop-op-counts` multiplies n × m over two loops; here the product runs over EVERY label, the cardinality-explosion postmortem in one formula.
hints: Each new label does not add series — it copies every existing series once per value it can take.
series = Π cardinalities (empty → 1); cents = series × centsPerSeries.
Each label multiplies the series count by its distinct values, so take the product across all labels — multiply by the per-series cents for the monthly bill

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · cost  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "We ingest 500 GB of logs a day and must keep them 90 days. Hot searchable storage costs 25¢ per GB-month and cold object storage 1¢. If we keep 7 days hot and demote the other 83 to cold, what is the monthly bill — and what does tiering save?"

**Why it works.** In steady state a tier that holds the last D days of logs stores gbPerDay × D GB at any moment, billed at that tier's cents per GB-month (money in integer cents). The bill is the sum over the tiers. Tiering saves the demoted volume (gbPerDay × coldDays) times the price gap between hot and cold.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `tieredMonthlyCents(gbPerDay, hotDays, hotCentsPerGb, coldDays, coldCentsPerGb)` → `gbPerDay × (hotDays × hotCentsPerGb + coldDays × coldCentsPerGb)`
- `savedByTieringCents(gbPerDay, coldDays, hotCentsPerGb, coldCentsPerGb)` → `gbPerDay × coldDays × (hotCentsPerGb − coldCentsPerGb)`

**Worked example.** Demoting 83 days of 500 GB/day saves 500 × 83 × (25 − 1) = **996,000¢** ($9,960) a month.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
One log stream, split by age, billed twice at very different prices.

For `tieredMonthlyCents(500, 7, 25, 83, 1)`:
- hot: 500 × 7 = 3,500 GB × 25¢ = 87,500¢
- cold: 500 × 83 = 41,500 GB × 1¢ = 41,500¢
- total → **129,000¢** ($1,290) against $11,250 keeping all 90 days hot

Demotion is the lever — module 10's `monthlyBillCents` adds two independent lines, while here ONE stream is split across tiers by age, plus the savings formula that justifies the split.
hints: At steady state each tier holds a fixed number of days of logs — price each tier's volume separately.
bill = gb/day × (hotDays × hot¢ + coldDays × cold¢); saved = gb/day × coldDays × (hot¢ − cold¢).
Steady-state storage per tier is gbPerDay × that tier's days, each billed at its own cents — the tiering saving is the demoted volume times the price gap, gbPerDay × coldDays × (hot − cold)

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** slo · alerting  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our SLO is 99.9% success over 30 days, so 1‰ of requests may fail. Right now 144‰ of requests are failing. How fast are we burning the error budget, and how many hours until a full month's budget is gone?"

**Why it works.** The burn rate is the observed failure per-mille divided by the budgeted failure per-mille: at 1× the budget lasts exactly the SLO window, and a 30-day window is 720 hours (30 × 24). Starting from a full budget, a burn rate of B× empties it in 720 ÷ B hours. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `burnRateX(actualFailPermille, budgetFailPermille)` → `actualFailPermille ÷ budgetFailPermille`
- `hoursToExhaust(burnRateX)` → `720 ÷ burnRateX`

**Worked example.** 10‰ failing against a 1‰ budget → a **10×** burn rate.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
A burn rate turns current behaviour into time-to-empty.

For `hoursToExhaust(144)`:
- a 30-day budget lasts 720 hours at 1×
- failing at 144× the allowed rate → 720 ÷ 144 = **5 hours**

That is why fast-burn alerts page within minutes and slow-burn alerts open tickets — module 03's `error-budget` converts an SLO into allowed minutes, while here the burn-rate MULTIPLIER converts what is happening now into hours left: the multi-window alert math.
hints: Compare how fast you are failing with how fast the budget allows — at exactly the allowed rate the budget lasts the whole window.
B = actual‰ ÷ budget‰; hours = 720 ÷ B.
The burn rate is the actual failure per-mille over the budget per-mille — a 30-day budget lasts 720 hours at 1×, so divide 720 by the burn rate for the hours left

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** alerting · operations  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our alerting evaluates 2,000 checks a day and about 5‰ of evaluations page someone for nothing. Each false page costs roughly 30 minutes of triage. How much on-call time does the noise burn per week?"

**Why it works.** False pages per day are the day's checks × the false-page per-mille ÷ 1000 (‰ = x/1000); a week is 7 of those days. Each page costs a fixed number of minutes, and 60 minutes make an hour. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `falsePagesPerWeek(checksPerDay, falsePagePermille)` → `checksPerDay × falsePagePermille × 7 ÷ 1000`
- `toilHoursPerWeek(falsePages, minutesPerPage)` → `falsePages × minutesPerPage ÷ 60`

**Worked example.** 600 checks/day at 10‰ → 600 × 10 × 7 ÷ 1000 = **42** false pages a week.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
Alert noise is paid for in engineer-hours.

For `toilHoursPerWeek(70, 30)`:
- 2,000 checks/day × 5‰ × 7 days = 70 false pages a week
- 70 × 30 minutes = 2,100 minutes ÷ 60 = **35 hours**

That is most of an engineer burned on noise — raise precision or delete checks. Module 04's `latency-slo-budget` budgets slow REQUESTS; here the budget is HUMAN: on-call hours consumed by false alarms.
hints: A small false-page rate times many evaluations times seven days is still a lot of interruptions — then price each one in minutes.
pages/week = checks/day × false‰ × 7 ÷ 1000; hours = pages × minutes ÷ 60.
False pages are the day's checks × the false per-mille ÷ 1000, times 7 days — multiply pages by the minutes each costs and divide by 60 for weekly toil hours

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · latency  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "One request creates 120 spans and each span costs about 10 µs to create, annotate and hand to the exporter. The endpoint answers in 40 ms. How big is the tracing tax, as a share of the request?"

**Why it works.** Span overhead in microseconds is spans × µs per span. As a share of latency in per-mille: overhead µs ÷ (requestMs × 1000 µs/ms) × 1000 — the two 1000s cancel, so overhead µs ÷ requestMs reads the tax directly in ‰ (1 ms = 1,000 µs). The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `overheadUsPerRequest(spans, usPerSpan)` → `spans × usPerSpan`
- `overheadPermilleOfLatency(spans, usPerSpan, requestMs)` → `spans × usPerSpan ÷ requestMs`

**Worked example.** 40 spans × 15 µs = **600 µs** of instrumentation per request.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
Instrumentation is a real latency tax, and it bites hardest on fast endpoints.

For `overheadPermilleOfLatency(120, 10, 40)`:
- 120 spans × 10 µs = 1,200 µs = 1.2 ms
- on a 40 ms request: 1,200 ÷ 40 = **30‰** (3%)

Module 01's `latency-budget` subtracts hop budgets from a total; here the instrumentation itself is the line item, as a share of one request.
hints: Add up what every span costs, then compare it with how long the request takes — watch the µs-to-ms conversion.
µs = spans × µs/span; ‰ = µs ÷ requestMs.
Span cost is spans × microseconds each — divide those microseconds by the request's milliseconds to read the tax directly in per-mille

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · storage  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "We keep 1,000 series. Raw scrapes run every 15 s; for a year of history we downsample to one point every 5 minutes. How many points does the year at 5-minute resolution store, and how does that compare with keeping raw?"

**Why it works.** A series produces one point per scrape, so 86,400 ÷ interval points a day (86,400 s/day). The store holds series × points per day × retention days. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `pointsPerDay(scrapeIntervalSec)` → `86400 ÷ scrapeIntervalSec`
- `pointsStored(series, scrapeIntervalSec, retentionDays)` → `series × 86400 × retentionDays ÷ scrapeIntervalSec`

**Worked example.** A 15 s scrape → 86,400 ÷ 15 = **5,760** points per series per day.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
Resolution, not series count, is the retention lever.

For `pointsStored(1000, 300, 365)`:
- 5-minute resolution → 86,400 ÷ 300 = 288 points per series per day
- 1,000 series × 288 × 365 days = **105,120,000** points for the year
- against 1,000 × 5,760 × 365 = 2,102,400,000 (2.1 billion) at raw 15 s

Module 01's `storage-growth` turns writes into bytes; here POINT counts are driven by scrape resolution — the downsampling decision.
hints: Every scrape adds one point to every series — count the scrapes in a day first.
points/day = 86,400 ÷ interval; stored = series × 86,400 × days ÷ interval.
A series produces 86,400 ÷ scrape-interval points per day — multiply by the series count and the retention days for what the TSDB must hold

sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.instructions:
**Skills:** observability · debugging  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "We serve 10,000,000 requests a day and 20,000 of them fail. Our head-based sampler keeps 5‰ of traces. How many error traces survive for debugging — and what would a tail sampler that keeps every error plus 5‰ of healthy traffic store instead?"

**Why it works.** A head sampler decides at the start of a request, before anyone knows how it will end, so errors are kept at the same per-mille as everything else (‰ = x/1000). A tail sampler buffers each trace until it completes, so it can keep EVERY error and apply the per-mille only to the healthy remainder (total − errors). The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `headErrorsKeptPerDay(errorsPerDay, samplePermille)` → `errorsPerDay × samplePermille ÷ 1000`
- `tailKeptPerDay(totalPerDay, errorsPerDay, samplePermille)` → `errorsPerDay + (totalPerDay − errorsPerDay) × samplePermille ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** Head sampling 20,000 errors at 5‰ → 20,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = **100** error traces kept.
sysdrills/14-observability-and-telemetry.explanation:
Sampling volume is one question; WHICH traces survive is the one debugging cares about.

For `tailKeptPerDay(10000000, 20000, 5)`:
- head sampling at 5‰ would keep only 20,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = 100 of the day's error traces
- tail keeps all 20,000 errors
- plus 5‰ of the 10,000,000 − 20,000 = 9,980,000 healthy traces = 49,900
- stored → **69,900** — 0.7% of the traffic, 100% of the failure evidence

Drill 14/01 sets the same dial's volume; here the question is which traces it keeps — and unlike module 02's weighted mix, one population is kept whole.
hints: Ask WHEN the keep-or-drop decision is made: before the outcome is known, or after the trace has finished.
head = errors × p ÷ 1000; tail = errors + (total − errors) × p ÷ 1000.
Head sampling keeps only the sampled per-mille of errors, errors × p ÷ 1000 — tail sampling keeps every error and adds the per-mille slice of the remaining (total − errors) traffic
